Twenty Third Indian Antarctic Expedition
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 21, pp 59-70
Study of Ambient Air Methane Concentration at 
Maitri, Antarctica
Pavan S. Kulkarni*1 * , S.L. Jain*, B.C. Arya+ , Sachin D Ghudef, Ashok Kumar1
and Shahnawaz*
tRadio and Atmospheric Sciences Division, National Physical Laboratory,
New Delhi -  110012 
JDept. of Physics and Astrophysics, University of Delhi,
Delhi - 110007
ABSTRACT
To study the ambient air concentration of methane at background site, 
measurement on hourly basis were carried out during the 23r d  IASE in the year 2004 
at Maitri, Antarctica (70° 45' S, 11° 45' E, 140 masl). Global warming studies require 
reliable estimates of true baseline values for greenhouse gases, which is only 
possible at some pristine location like Antarctica. Measurement of CH4  made for a 
period of 22 months showed that the day-to-day variation was small except the 
variation of few ppb. No diurnal variation has been observed. About 83% of CH4  
values have been observed in the range of 1.685 ppmv to 1.715 ppmv during the 
entire period of measurement from February 2003 to December 2004.
The ambient air surface concentration of CH4  during the period of observation 
was found to be nearly stable. Annual mean concentration of 1.699 ppmv for CH4  
has been observed in 2003 with standard deviation of 13 ppbv and 1.701 ppmv in 
2004 with standard deviation of 6 ppbv. Mean CH4  concentration for 22 month 
period has been observed at 1.7 ppmv with standard deviation of 9 ppbv. The 
observed stable CH4  concentration indicates a decrease in emissions, which may 
have forced the global methane budget towards a steady state.
Keywords: Methane; Antarctica; Global warming; baseline values
INTRODUCTION
The distribution of greenhouse gases (GHGs) in the atmosphere, 
particularly those due to human and biosphere activities, is quite 
heterogeneous (Mukhopadhyay et al, 2002). Increase in the atmospheric 
concentration of GHGs such as carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide,

halo-carbons and tropospheric ozone since the industrial period (1750) has 
been identified as one of the major causes of the warming of the earth’s 
surface (Hansen et al, 1998; Lacis et al, 1981; Wang et al, 1976). C 0 2  has 
the largest radiative effect. Now it has been recognized that the global 
warming due to infrared active gases like 0 3 , CFCs, CH4 , Nz O, etc. is 
collectively as much as that due to C 02  alone (Jain et al, 2000), where as it 
was only due to C 02  during the pre-industrial era upto 1950s. Next to carbon 
dioxide, methane is the most abundant and important organic trace gas in 
the atmosphere. It absorbs infrared radiation (Lelieveld et al, 1998) and is 
also involved in tropospheric and stratospheric photochemical reactions 
(Lelieveld and Crutzen, 1992). The major natural sources of Methane are 
natural wetlands, termites and oceans and anthropogenic sources are rice 
paddies, energy landfills, ruminants, waste treatment and biomass burning 
(IPCC, 2001; Schimel et al, 1996). The main sink of atmospheric methane 
is the reaction with OH radical (Singh et al, 1995):
OH + CH4  ---------> CH3  + H2 0  . (6.1)
The reaction is rather slow and, as a result, the atmospheric lifetime 
of methane is long. Recent process model study by Ridgwell (1999) suggested 
that soil sinks CH4  of approximately 30Tg/yr. Similarly, stratospheric loss 
is another minor sink of methane (Hein et al, 1997). Methane has strong 
absorption band at 3.3 pm and 7.66 pm and trap part of the thermal radiation 
from the earth’s surface (Wang et al, 1976). Lelieveld et al (1998) and Jain 
et al (2000) estimated that the current direct radiative forcing of 0.48 
Wm'2  from CH4  is 20% of the total from all of the long-lived and globally 
mixed greenhouse gases. Based on the reaction rate coefficient between 
CH4  and OH, and the estimated tropospheric distribution of OH, Prinn et al 
(1995) derived a mean atmospheric lifetime for CH4  of 8.9 years. In the 
stratosphere, methane is a source of water vapor and hydrogen and controls 
the abundance of Cl atoms converting them to HC1 as,
Cl + CH4  ---------> CH3  + HC1 (6.2)
Although some of the hydrogen is produced by CH4 , most of the CH4  
molecule transported into stratosphere produces water vapor by oxidation. 
Craig and Chou (1982) observed that, in the distant past, variations in natural 
sources of methane were responsible for trends in atmospheric methane 
levels recorded in ice cores. On the basis of analysis of ancient air trapped
